Three or more actor groups

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/multigroup.Rmd
multigroup.Rmd

Many learning settings involve more than two kinds of actor. A student working with an AI assistant inside a programming environment interacts with the assistant and with the environment itself, whose compiler messages, notifications and logs are events of a third kind. A classroom dialogue can involve a teacher, students and a conversational agent. Heterogeneous transition network analysis does not depend on there being two actors: the actor partition can have any number of groups, and the weight matrix is then partitioned into one block for every ordered pair of actors. With three actors there are three within-actor blocks and six between-actor blocks, so the question of who hands over to whom has six answers instead of two.

This guide builds a three-actor network, reads its actor-pair structure, draws it in the layouts available for several groups, counts the three-actor meta-paths, and compares two networks. Every function used for two actors works unchanged.

library(htna)

Data

The package has no bundled data with three actor types, so the guide uses a small simulated study of 30 sessions in which a Student, an AI assistant and a System (the programming environment) act in turn. Each actor has four codes.

  • Student: Ask, Confirm, Revise, Evaluate.
  • AI: Suggest, Explain, Execute, Clarify.
  • System: Log, Notify, Compile, Sync.
  • Session and order: session_id and order_in_session. In each session the three actors act in the fixed cycle Student, AI, System for as long as each has events (15 to 25 per actor and session), and the codes within an actor are drawn at random.

The turn order is therefore built into the data, and the codes carry no structure. The analyses below should recover the cycle and nothing else.

set.seed(42)
student_codes <- c("Ask", "Confirm", "Revise", "Evaluate")
ai_codes      <- c("Suggest", "Explain", "Execute", "Clarify")
system_codes  <- c("Log", "Notify", "Compile", "Sync")
sessions      <- sprintf("S%03d", seq_len(30))

make_events <- function(codes, sessions, offset) {
  rows <- lapply(sessions, function(sid) {
    n <- sample(15:25, 1)
    data.frame(session_id = sid, code = sample(codes, n, replace = TRUE),
               order_in_session = seq_len(n) * 3L - offset)
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}

student_data <- make_events(student_codes, sessions, 2L)
ai_data      <- make_events(ai_codes, sessions, 1L)
system_data  <- make_events(system_codes, sessions, 0L)

Building a network with three actors

The three tables are passed as a named list; the names become the actor types, in the order given. A single table with an actor column or a codebook works in the same way (see Input formats).

net3 <- build_htna(list(Student = student_data, AI = ai_data,
                        System = system_data))
summary(net3)
#> <htna network>
#>   Method:    relative
#>   Sessions:  30   (max 70 timesteps)
#>   Nodes:     12
#>   Edges:     116 / 144 (non-zero)
#> 
#> Actor types (3):
#>   Student (4 nodes):  Ask, Confirm, Evaluate, Revise
#>   AI      (4 nodes):  Clarify, Execute, Explain, Suggest
#>   System  (4 nodes):  Compile, Log, Notify, Sync
#> 
#> Edge counts by actor (rows = source, cols = target):
#>             Student      AI  System
#>   Student         3      16      14
#>   AI             13       9      16
#>   System         16      15      14
#> 
#> Network metrics:
#>                       metric    value
#>                   Node Count  12.0000
#>                   Edge Count 116.0000
#>              Network Density   0.8788
#>                Mean Distance   0.0188
#>            Mean Out-Strength   1.0000
#>              SD Out-Strength   0.0000
#>             Mean In-Strength   1.0000
#>               SD In-Strength   0.0916
#>              Mean Out-Degree   9.6667
#>                SD Out-Degree   1.5570
#>  Centralization (Out-Degree)   0.1818
#>   Centralization (In-Degree)   0.1818
#>                  Reciprocity   0.8727

The network has 12 nodes, four per actor, and 116 of its 144 possible edges are non-zero. The edge counts by actor form a three-by-three table. As a tidy table, one row per directed actor pair:

as.data.frame(summary(net3), what = "actor_pairs")
#>   source_actor target_actor n_edges
#> 1      Student      Student       3
#> 2      Student           AI      16
#> 3      Student       System      14
#> 4           AI      Student      13
#> 5           AI           AI       9
#> 6           AI       System      16
#> 7       System      Student      16
#> 8       System           AI      15
#> 9       System       System      14

The block structure reflects the turn cycle: the Student-to-Student block has only 3 non-zero edges, because a student event is followed by another student event only where the other actors have run out of events, while the blocks of the cycle (Student to AI, AI to System, System to Student) have 16 each, all possible edges. The other blocks are filled at the ends of sessions, where the remaining actors continue among themselves.

Drawing three actor groups

With the default circular layout each actor occupies one arc of the circle, coloured and shaped by actor.

plot_htna(net3)

layout = "polygon" places each actor along one side of a regular polygon, a triangle for three actors, which separates the groups more clearly.

plot_htna(net3, layout = "polygon")

Which three-actor templates recur?

extract_meta_paths() at the type level counts runs of actor types. With three actors there are 27 possible templates of length three.

print(extract_meta_paths(net3, level = "type", length = 3), n = 6)
#> Meta-paths (type-level) over 30 sequences
#> Rows: 17 | Lengths: 3 | Gaps: 0
#>                   schema length gap count n_seq support frequency lift
#>      Student->AI->System      3   0   510    30   1.000     0.295 7.98
#>      AI->System->Student      3   0   497    30   1.000     0.288 7.78
#>      System->Student->AI      3   0   487    30   1.000     0.282 7.62
#>           AI->System->AI      3   0    41    10   0.333     0.024 0.62
#>       System->AI->System      3   0    37    10   0.333     0.021 0.56
#>  System->Student->System      3   0    32    10   0.333     0.019 0.50
#> ... (11 more)

The three rotations of the cycle (Student->AI->System, AI->System->Student, System->Student->AI) occur in all 30 sessions and account for 0.295, 0.288 and 0.282 of the runs, about eight times as often as expected from the actors’ overall shares (lift 7.62 to 7.98). The next most frequent template, AI->System->AI, occurs 41 times in 10 sessions, less often than expected (lift 0.62). The meta-paths recover the built-in turn order exactly. A schema returns the concrete instances of one template:

print(extract_meta_paths(net3, schema = "Student->AI->System"), n = 6)
#> State-level instances of schema 'Student->AI->System' over 30 sequences
#> Rows: 64 | Lengths: 3 | Gaps: 0
#>                      schema         meta_schema length gap count n_seq support frequency
#>   Confirm->Clarify->Compile Student->AI->System      3   0    15    14   0.467     0.029
#>   Confirm->Execute->Compile Student->AI->System      3   0    13    12   0.400     0.025
#>  Evaluate->Explain->Compile Student->AI->System      3   0    13    12   0.400     0.025
#>      Confirm->Suggest->Sync Student->AI->System      3   0    13    11   0.367     0.025
#>        Ask->Explain->Notify Student->AI->System      3   0    12    11   0.367     0.024
#>    Confirm->Explain->Notify Student->AI->System      3   0    12    12   0.400     0.024
#>   lift
#>  11.86
#>  10.08
#>  13.00
#>  12.66
#>  11.07
#>   9.53
#> ... (58 more)

All 64 combinations of four codes per actor occur, and because the codes within each actor were drawn at random they have similar counts (the most frequent, Confirm->Clarify->Compile, occurs 15 times); no particular student move leads to a particular AI move. Their high lifts come from the turn cycle, not from the codes.

Do two samples from the same process differ?

A second set of 30 sessions is simulated from the same process. A permutation test of the two networks should find no difference.

set.seed(7)
net3b <- build_htna(list(
  Student = make_events(student_codes, sessions, 2L),
  AI      = make_events(ai_codes, sessions, 1L),
  System  = make_events(system_codes, sessions, 0L)
))
perm3 <- permutation_htna(net3, net3b, iter = 200, seed = 1)
perm3
#> Permutation Test: Transition Network (relative probabilities) [directed]
#>   Iterations: 200  |  Alpha: 0.05
#>   Nodes: 12  |  Edges tested: 136  |  Significant: 2
#>   Global test (networks differ overall?): M = 2.693 (p = 0.587)  |  S = 0.103 (p = 0.846)

The global test finds no difference (M = 2.693, p = 0.587; S = 0.103, p = 0.846), and 2 of the 136 tested edges fall below 0.05, fewer than the seven expected by chance at that level. The test behaves as it should when the two networks come from one process. The difference network draws the two nominally significant edges:

plot_htna_diff(perm3)

With show_nonsig = TRUE, the non-significant differences are added as dashed edges.

plot_htna_diff(perm3, show_nonsig = TRUE)

What changes with more actors

Step Two actors Three or more actors
Actor-pair blocks 4 the number of actors squared (9 for three)
Layout circular, two arcs circular arcs, or layout = "polygon"
Meta-paths of length three 8 templates the number of actors cubed (27 for three)
Comparison and assessment compare_htna(), permutation_htna(), bootstrap_htna() unchanged

The number of blocks and templates grows quickly with the number of actors, so more sessions are needed to estimate every block; the actor-pair table of summary() shows which blocks rest on few edges.
